claim: The non-neuronal ENS cell compartment of teleosts shares molecular and morphological characteristics with mammalian enteric glia.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the non-neuronal ENS cell compartment of teleosts shares molecular and morphological characteristics with mammalian enteric glia but cannot be identified by the expression of canonical glial markers.
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic analysis showing gene expression overlap (Figure 2), morphological analysis showing four EGC subtypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and ultrastructural features (Figure 4).

claim: The non-neuronal ENS cell compartment of teleosts cannot be identified by the expression of canonical glial markers.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the non-neuronal ENS cell compartment of teleosts shares molecular and morphological characteristics with mammalian enteric glia but cannot be identified by the expression of canonical glial markers.
evidence: Immunostaining for S100β, GFAP, BFABP, and nestin:GFP transgene expression were undetectable in zebrafish ENS (Figure 1D-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Unlike mammalian enteric glia, which are generally quiescent and do not undergo neuronal differentiation during homeostasis, a relatively high proportion of zebrafish enteric glia proliferate under physiological conditions.
source: However, unlike their mammalian counterparts, which are generally quiescent and do not undergo neuronal differentiation during homeostasis, we show that a relatively high proportion of zebrafish enteric glia proliferate under physiological conditions giving rise to progeny that differentiate into enteric neurons.
evidence: 10.8 ± 4.2% of GFP+ cells were positive for MCM5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and 8.0 ± 4.3% of GFP+ cells were co-labelled with EdU (Figure 6A,B,D).

claim: Zebrafish enteric glia give rise to progeny that differentiate into enteric neurons.
source: However, unlike their mammalian counterparts, which are generally quiescent and do not undergo neuronal differentiation during homeostasis, we show that a relatively high proportion of zebrafish enteric glia proliferate under physiological conditions giving rise to progeny that differentiate into enteric neurons.
evidence: EdU labelling experiments showed increased percentage of EdU+ enteric neurons at t4 and t11 relative to t0 (Figure 6E), and EdU+ doublets including GFP+HuC/D- and GFP-HuC/D+ cells were identified (Figure 6C).

claim: The activation and neuronal differentiation of zebrafish enteric glia are regulated by Notch signalling.
source: We also provide evidence that, similar to brain neural stem cells, the activation and neuronal differentiation of enteric glia are regulated by Notch signalling.
evidence: LY411575 treatment resulted in dramatic increase in proliferation of non-neuronal ENS cells (Figure 7B,D) and increased enteric neurogenesis (Figure 7C,E).

claim: The majority of GFP+ cells (93.76% ± 2.99) in 7 dpf SAGFF234A;UAS:GFP larvae co-expressed the pan-neuronal marker HuC/D.
source: In 7 day post fertilisation (dpf) larvae the majority of GFP+ cells (93.76% ± 2.99) co-expressed the pan-neuronal marker HuC/D (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,D), suggesting that in comparison to mammals, in which EGCs outnumber enteric neurons (Gabella, 1981; Rühl, 2005), the non-neuronal ENS cell population of zebrafish is considerably smaller.
evidence: Quantification from immunostaining of SAGFF234A;UAS:GFP larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,D).

claim: In mammals, EGCs outnumber enteric neurons.
source: In 7 day post fertilisation (dpf) larvae the majority of GFP+ cells (93.76% ± 2.99) co-expressed the pan-neuronal marker HuC/D (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,D), suggesting that in comparison to mammals, in which EGCs outnumber enteric neurons (Gabella, 1981; Rühl, 2005), the non-neuronal ENS cell population of zebrafish is considerably smaller.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Gabella, 1981; Rühl, 2005).

claim: The non-neuronal ENS cell population of zebrafish is considerably smaller than in mammals.
source: In 7 day post fertilisation (dpf) larvae the majority of GFP+ cells (93.76% ± 2.99) co-expressed the pan-neuronal marker HuC/D (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,D), suggesting that in comparison to mammals, in which EGCs outnumber enteric neurons (Gabella, 1981; Rühl, 2005), the non-neuronal ENS cell population of zebrafish is considerably smaller.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 93.76% of ENS cells are neurons in zebrafish, compared to mammals where glia outnumber neurons.

claim: The majority of Cherry+ cells (84.79 ± 7.70%) in the gut of 7 dpf Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) larvae were positive for HuC/D.
source: Consistent with the analysis of SAGFF234A;UAS:GFP animals, the majority of Cherry+ cells (84.79 ± 7.70%) in the gut of 7 dpf Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) larvae were positive for HuC/D (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: Quantification from immunostaining shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: In adult (≥3 months old) Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish, the majority of ENS+ cells (65.49 ± 4.8%) were neurons.
source: Similar analysis in adult (≥3 months old) Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish showed that, although the fraction of non-neuronal Cherry+ cells was higher relative to 7 dpf larvae, even at this stage the majority of ENS+ cells (65.49 ± 4.8%) were neurons (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Quantification from immunostaining shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: No S100β signal was detected in the ENS of 7 dpf zebrafish larvae.
source: Surprisingly, no signal was detected in the ENS of zebrafish at this stage (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Immunostaining with S100β antibody showed no ENS-specific signal (Figure 1D).

claim: Expression of the Tg(gfap:GFP) transgene was undetectable in the gut of 7 dpf larvae.
source: Consistent with the immunostaining, expression of the Tg(gfap:GFP) transgene (Bernardos and Raymond, 2006) was also undetectable in the gut of 7 dpf larvae (Figure 1E).
evidence: Analysis of Tg(gfap:GFP) larvae showed no GFP expression in the gut (Figure 1E).

claim: No apparent ENS-specific expression of GFAP, S100β, BFABP or gfap:GFP transgene was detected in adult zebrafish gut.
source: Similar to 7 dpf animals, no apparent ENS-specific expression of these markers or the gfap:GFP transgene was detected in the adult gut (Figure 1F–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q–R).
evidence: Immunostaining of adult gut showed no ENS-specific signal for these markers (Figure 1F–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q–R).

claim: No expression of the nestin:GFP transgene was detected in the ENS of adult zebrafish.
source: Finally, contrary to reports indicating expression of Nestin in non-neuronal cells of mammalian enteric ganglia (Kulkarni et al., 2017), no expression of the nestin:GFP transgene was detected in the ENS of adult zebrafish (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S).
evidence: Analysis of Tg(nestin:GFP) adult zebrafish showed no GFP expression in the ENS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S).

claim: Genes associated with non-NC tissues were upregulated in the Cherry- nuclear transcriptome.
source: As expected, genes associated with non-NC tissues, such as smooth muscle cells (myh11a, cald1a, srfa, gata6), interstitial cells of Cajal (ano1, kita, kitb) and immune cells (lcp1, lck, lyz), were upregulated in the Cherry- nuclear transcriptome (Figure 2B).
evidence: Bulk nRNAseq analysis showed differential gene expression between Cherry+ and Cherry- populations (Figure 2B).

claim: Genes associated with the NC-derived ENS lineages were upregulated in the Cherry+ nuclear population.
source: Conversely, genes associated with the NC-derived ENS lineages (such as elavl3, elavl4, ret, vip, chata, sox10) were upregulated in the Cherry+ nuclear population (Figure 2B) (GEO database GSE145885; Supplementary file 1; an interactive data viewer to explore the analysed data can be found here: https://biologic.crick.ac.uk/ENS).
evidence: Bulk nRNAseq analysis showed differential gene expression between Cherry+ and Cherry- populations (Figure 2B).

claim: GO terms enriched in the Cherry+ nuclear population were associated with nervous system development and function.
source: Furthermore, gene ontology (GO) terms enriched in the Cherry+ nuclear population were associated with nervous system development and function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis of Cherry+ transcriptome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).

claim: sox10 is expressed specifically by non-neuronal ENS cells in adult zebrafish.
source: Expression of sox10, foxd3 and sox2 in the non-neuronal compartment of the zebrafish ENS was validated by combining multiplex fluorescence in situ hybridisation (RNAscope) with immunostaining for HuC/D and the Cherry reporter on muscularis externa preparations from the gut of adult Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: RNAscope analysis showed sox10 signal in Cherry+HuC/D- cells (Figure 2D).

claim: foxd3 is expressed specifically by non-neuronal ENS cells in adult zebrafish.
source: Expression of sox10, foxd3 and sox2 in the non-neuronal compartment of the zebrafish ENS was validated by combining multiplex fluorescence in situ hybridisation (RNAscope) with immunostaining for HuC/D and the Cherry reporter on muscularis externa preparations from the gut of adult Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: RNAscope analysis showed foxd3 signal in Cherry+HuC/D- cells (Figure 2E).

claim: Sox2 is expressed specifically by non-neuronal ENS cells in adult zebrafish.
source: Expression of sox10, foxd3 and sox2 in the non-neuronal compartment of the zebrafish ENS was validated by combining multiplex fluorescence in situ hybridisation (RNAscope) with immunostaining for HuC/D and the Cherry reporter on muscularis externa preparations from the gut of adult Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Immunostaining showed Sox2 expression in Cherry+HuC/D- cells (Figure 2F).

claim: The Notch activity reporter Tg(her4.3:EGFP) marks NSCs and neural progenitors in the zebrafish brain.
source: Moreover, the transgenic Notch activity reporter Tg(her4.3:EGFP) (see Materials and Methods for the nomenclature of this transgene) marks NSCs and neural progenitors in the zebrafish brain (Alunni and Bally-Cuif, 2016; Yeo et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Alunni and Bally-Cuif, 2016; Yeo et al., 2007).

claim: A network of GFP+ cells was identified in the muscularis externa of adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP) zebrafish gut that was closely associated with enteric neurons and their projections.
source: This analysis identified a network of GFP+ cells in the muscularis externa of the gut that was closely associated with enteric neurons and their projections (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunostaining of adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP) gut showed GFP+ cells associated with HuC/D+ neurons (Figure 3A).

claim: GFP+ cells in adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish were negative for HuC/D but expressed the Cherry reporter.
source: As expected, GFP+ cells were negative for HuC/D but expressed the Cherry reporter (Figure 3C), indicating that they belong to the non-neuronal compartment of the ENS.
evidence: Immunostaining showed GFP+HuC/D-Cherry+ cells (Figure 3C).

claim: GFP+ cells co-expressed sox2 and sox10 in adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish.
source: Consistent with this idea, GFP+ cells co-expressed sox2 and sox10 (Figure 3D,E), which were identified by our transcriptomic analysis as genes expressed by the non-neuronal compartment of the zebrafish ENS.
evidence: Immunostaining and RNAscope showed GFP+ cells expressing Sox2 and sox10 (Figure 3D,E).

claim: Sox2 was widely expressed in the GFP+HuC/D- cell population in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) tissue.
source: We observed heterogeneity within the non-neuronal component: whereas Sox2 was widely expressed in the GFP+HuC/D- cell population in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) tissue, foxd3 was expressed in only a proportion of the GFP+HuC/D-/Sox2+ cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: Combined RNAscope and immunostaining showed widespread Sox2 expression in GFP+ cells (Figure 3F).

claim: foxd3 was expressed in only a proportion of the GFP+HuC/D-/Sox2+ cells in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) tissue.
source: We observed heterogeneity within the non-neuronal component: whereas Sox2 was widely expressed in the GFP+HuC/D- cell population in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) tissue, foxd3 was expressed in only a proportion of the GFP+HuC/D-/Sox2+ cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: Combined RNAscope and immunostaining showed foxd3 expression in a subset of GFP+Sox2+ cells (Figure 3F).

claim: The GFP+HuC/D- cell population in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) represented approximately a quarter (24.20 ± 5.18%) of all Cherry+ ENS cells.
source: The GFP+HuC/D- cell population in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) represented approximately a quarter (24.20 ± 5.18%) of all Cherry+ ENS cells, but 12.93 ± 5.33% of Cherry+ cells were negative for both GFP and HuC/D (Cherry+GFP-HuC/D-) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Quantification from immunostaining of adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish (Figure 3B).

claim: 12.93 ± 5.33% of Cherry+ cells were negative for both GFP and HuC/D (Cherry+GFP-HuC/D-) in adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish.
source: The GFP+HuC/D- cell population in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) represented approximately a quarter (24.20 ± 5.18%) of all Cherry+ ENS cells, but 12.93 ± 5.33% of Cherry+ cells were negative for both GFP and HuC/D (Cherry+GFP-HuC/D-) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Quantification from immunostaining of adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish (Figure 3B).

claim: GFP+ cells in Tg(her4.3:EGFP) zebrafish fell into four morphological groups that generally corresponded to the four morphological subtypes of mouse EGCs (Types I-IV).
source: At the light microscopy level GFP+ cells were highly branched and fell into four morphological groups that generally corresponded to the four morphological subtypes of mouse EGCs (Types I-IV) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E; Boesmans et al., 2015; Gulbransen and Sharkey, 2012).
evidence: Morphological analysis of GFP+ cells showed four distinct types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E) similar to mammalian EGC subtypes described in literature (Boesmans et al., 2015; Gulbransen and Sharkey, 2012).

claim: Processes emanating from EGFP+ cells could extend to 18 µm and directly contacted enteric neurons.
source: Processes emanating from EGFP+ cells could extend to 18 µm and directly contacted enteric neurons (Figure 4B,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but similar to mammalian EGCs (Gabella, 1981) they did not form complete 'capsules' around neuronal somata, allowing large parts of enteric neurons to be in direct contact with adjacent cells (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Video 1).
evidence: CLEM analysis showed EGFP+ cell processes extending up to 18 µm and contacting neurons (Figure 4B,D).

claim: EGFP+ cells did not form complete 'capsules' around neuronal somata, similar to mammalian EGCs.
source: Processes emanating from EGFP+ cells could extend to 18 µm and directly contacted enteric neurons (Figure 4B,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but similar to mammalian EGCs (Gabella, 1981) they did not form complete 'capsules' around neuronal somata, allowing large parts of enteric neurons to be in direct contact with adjacent cells (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Video 1).
evidence: CLEM analysis showed incomplete coverage of neurons by EGFP+ cell processes (Figure 4A,B, Video 1), consistent with mammalian EGCs (Gabella, 1981).

claim: EGFP+ cells extended complex sheet-like extensions which frequently enclosed and/or subdivided tightly packed bundles of neural projections into sectors.
source: EGFP+ cells also extended complex sheet-like extensions, which frequently enclosed and/or subdivided the tightly packed bundles of neural projections into sectors (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Video 1).
evidence: CLEM analysis showed EGFP+ cells with sheet-like extensions compartmentalizing axon bundles (Figure 4D, Video 1).

claim: Scarcity of cytoplasm and deep nuclear crenations were found in the nuclei of EGFP+ cells.
source: Scarcity of cytoplasm and deep nuclear crenations, characteristic features of mammalian EGCs and other populations of peripheral glial cells (Gabella, 1981), were also found in the nuclei of EGFP+ cells (Figure 4B,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: CLEM analysis showed nuclear crenations in EGFP+ cells (Figure 4B,D), similar to mammalian EGCs (Gabella, 1981).

claim: At 54 hpf, no double positive (Cherry+GFP+) cells were identified in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;SAGFF234A;UAS:mmCherry) embryos.
source: At 54 hr post fertilisation (hpf), a stage at which NC cell-derived Cherry+ cells are restricted to two distinct migratory columns along the gut (Heanue et al., 2016a), no double positive (Cherry+GFP+) cells were identified (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Analysis of fixed embryos showed no Cherry+GFP+ cells at 54 hpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: At 60 hpf, a small number of GFP+ cells were discernible within the Cherry+ streams of NC cells in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;SAGFF234A;UAS:mmCherry) embryos.
source: However, at 60 hpf a small number of GFP+ cells were discernible within the Cherry+ streams of NC cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and became more abundant in 4 dpf larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Analysis of fixed embryos showed GFP+ cells within Cherry+ NC cell streams at 60 hpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: EGFP+ cells appeared within the columns of mmCherry+ cells at around 62 hpf during live imaging.
source: Consistent with the analysis performed on fixed embryos, no EGFP+ cells were identified within the mmCherry+ population during the first hours of imaging (Figure 5A). However, EGFP+ cells appeared within the columns of mmCherry+ cells at around 62 hpf (Figure 5B), more than 90 µm behind the front of migrating mmCherry+ NC cells, and the number of EGFP+ cells increased over the remaining imaging period (Figure 5C,D; Video 2).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging showed first EGFP+ cells appearing at 62 hpf (Figure 5B, Video 2).

claim: EGFP+ cells appeared more than 90 µm behind the front of migrating mmCherry+ NC cells.
source: However, EGFP+ cells appeared within the columns of mmCherry+ cells at around 62 hpf (Figure 5B), more than 90 µm behind the front of migrating mmCherry+ NC cells, and the number of EGFP+ cells increased over the remaining imaging period (Figure 5C,D; Video 2).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging showed EGFP+ cells appearing behind the migratory front (Figure 5B, Video 2).

claim: Individual mmCherry+ cells were observed inducing de novo expression of EGFP during live imaging.
source: On several occasions, we identified individual mmCherry+ cells inducing de novo expression of EGFP (Video 3).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging captured de novo EGFP expression in mmCherry+ cells (Video 3).

claim: EGFP+ cells on average exhibited minimal rostrocaudal displacement relative to the tip of the mmCherry+ migratory column.
source: Relative to the tip of the mmCherry+ migratory column, which was displaced caudally at a constant rate until it reached the caudal end of the FOV, EGFP+ cells on average exhibited minimal rostrocaudal displacement (Figure 5E; 132 EGFP+ cells analysed from four fish), suggesting that during ENS development the her4.3:EGFP transgene is expressed in post-migratory cells.
evidence: Quantification of cell displacement from time-lapse imaging (Figure 5E).

claim: During ENS development, the her4.3:EGFP transgene is expressed in post-migratory cells.
source: Relative to the tip of the mmCherry+ migratory column, which was displaced caudally at a constant rate until it reached the caudal end of the FOV, EGFP+ cells on average exhibited minimal rostrocaudal displacement (Figure 5E; 132 EGFP+ cells analysed from four fish), suggesting that during ENS development the her4.3:EGFP transgene is expressed in post-migratory cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EGFP+ cells showed minimal displacement compared to the migrating wavefront (Figure 5E).

claim: Of 79 EGFP+ cells analyzed during live imaging, 37 cells gave rise to at least one generation of GFP+ progeny.
source: Next, we characterised the cell division patterns of the 79 EGFP+ cells that migrated into the field of view or arose de novo during the live imaging period. Of these, 37 cells gave rise to at least one generation of GFP+ progeny.
evidence: Analysis of time-lapse imaging data tracking individual EGFP+ cells.

claim: 26 EGFP+ cells (~33%) underwent a single cell division generating two daughters during live imaging.
source: 26 cells (~33%) underwent a single cell division generating two daughters, many of which lost EGFP expression over the course of imaging.
evidence: Analysis of time-lapse imaging data tracking individual EGFP+ cells.

claim: 53 EGFP+ cells were seen to undergo a cell division event during the imaging period.
source: Altogether, 53 EGFP+ cells were seen to undergo a cell division event during the imaging period.
evidence: Analysis of time-lapse imaging data tracking individual EGFP+ cells.

claim: Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expressing cells undergo only a limited number of cell divisions during development.
source: Therefore, during development Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expressing cells are capable of entering the cell cycle but those that do so undergo only a limited number of cell divisions and many of their progeny eventually lose expression of EGFP.
evidence: Analysis of time-lapse imaging showed cells undergoing 1-3 divisions with progeny losing EGFP expression.

claim: Many progeny of dividing Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expressing cells eventually lose expression of EGFP during development.
source: Therefore, during development Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expressing cells are capable of entering the cell cycle but those that do so undergo only a limited number of cell divisions and many of their progeny eventually lose expression of EGFP.
evidence: Analysis of time-lapse imaging showed progeny of dividing cells losing EGFP expression.

claim: Loss of EGFP signal could be associated with neuronal differentiation.
source: Loss of EGFP signal could be associated with neuronal differentiation, since we occasionally identified in the gut of 7 dpf her4.3:EGFP transgenic larvae cells that were weakly immunostained for both HuC/D and GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Observation of cells weakly positive for both HuC/D and GFP in 7 dpf larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).

claim: 10.8 ± 4.2% of GFP+ cells in adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP) zebrafish were positive for MCM5.
source: 10.8 ± 4.2% of GFP+ cells were positive for MCM5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that in contrast to their mammalian counterparts, a considerable proportion of zebrafish EGCs are cycling during homeostasis.
evidence: Quantification from immunostaining of adult Tg(her4.3:EGFP) gut (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: A considerable proportion of zebrafish EGCs are cycling during homeostasis, in contrast to their mammalian counterparts.
source: 10.8 ± 4.2% of GFP+ cells were positive for MCM5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that in contrast to their mammalian counterparts, a considerable proportion of zebrafish EGCs are cycling during homeostasis.
evidence: 10.8% MCM5+ cells compared to mammalian EGCs which are generally quiescent (Joseph et al., 2011).

claim: At the end of a 3 day EdU labelling pulse (t0), 8.0 ± 4.3% of GFP+ cells in adult her4.3:EGFP transgenic zebrafish were co-labelled with EdU.
source: Consistent with the MCM5 immunostaining, we found that at the end of a 3 day EdU labelling pulse (t0), 8.0 ± 4.3% of GFP+ cells in the gut of 3 month old her4.3:EGFP transgenic zebrafish were co-labelled with EdU (Figure 6A,B and D).
evidence: Quantification from EdU labelling experiment (Figure 6A,B,D).

claim: Tg(her4.3:EGFP) cells represent a largely quiescent cell population with dividing cells having long cell cycles.
source: The similar percentage of MCM5+ and EdU+ cells suggests that Tg(her4.3:EGFP) cells represent a largely quiescent cell population and the that dividing cells have long cell cycles.
evidence: Inferred from the similar percentages of MCM5+ (10.8%) and EdU+ (8.0%) cells.

claim: The majority of (GFP+EdU+) cells at t0 formed doublets composed of cells with similar morphology and GFP signal intensity.
source: In these experiments, the majority of (GFP+EdU+) cells formed doublets composed of cells with similar morphology and GFP signal intensity (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Observation from EdU labelling experiments (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).

claim: EdU+ doublets including GFP+HuC/D- and GFP-HuC/D+ cells were identified 4 days post-labelling (t4 chase).
source: This idea was supported by the identification 4 days post-labelling (t4 chase) of EdU+ doublets that included GFP+HuC/D- and GFP-HuC/D+ cells (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: Observation from EdU chase experiments (Figure 6A,C).

claim: The percentage of EdU+GFP+ cells was reduced at t4 (3.6 ± 3.4%, p=6.01×10−7) and t11 (3.9 ± 3.8%, p=7.61×10−6) compared to t0.
source: The loss of GFP signal from the daughters of proliferating EGCs cells was also supported by cell population analysis which demonstrated a reduction in the percentage of EdU+GFP+ cells (t4: 3.6 ± 3.4%, p=6.01×10−7; t11: 3.9 ± 3.8%, p=7.61×10−6) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Quantification from EdU chase experiments (Figure 6D).

claim: The reduced percentage of EdU+GFP+ cells during the EdU chase period was associated with a concomitant increase in the representation of EdU+ enteric neurons at t4 (0.71 ± 0.80%, p=6.0×10−7) and t11 (0.70 ± 0.82%, p=1.5×10−6) relative to t0 (0.068 ± 0.13%).
source: Interestingly, the reduced percentage of EdU+GFP+ cells during the EdU chase period was associated with a concomitant increase in the representation of EdU+ enteric neurons at t4 (0.71 ± 0.80%, p=6.0×10−7) and t11 (0.70 ± 0.82%, p=1.5×10−6) relative to t0 (0.068 ± 0.13%) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Quantification from EdU chase experiments (Figure 6E).

claim: The progeny of proliferating EGCs in the zebrafish ENS can differentiate into neurons under physiological conditions.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that the progeny of proliferating EGCs in the zebrafish ENS can differentiate into neurons under physiological conditions.
evidence: Inferred from EdU chase experiments showing loss of GFP and gain of HuC/D in EdU+ cells (Figure 6C-E).

claim: The actual densities of GFP+EdU+ and HuC/D+ EdU+ cells were significantly higher within smaller radius circles (<60 µm) compared to those expected by chance.
source: This analysis revealed that the actual densities of GFP+EdU+ and HuC/D+ EdU+ cells were significantly higher within the smaller radius circles (<60 µm from the cell of interest) in comparison to those expected by chance, suggesting that the observed homotypic (GFP+EdU+/GFP+EdU+) and heterotypic (GFP+EdU+/HuC/D+EdU+) clusters of EdU+ ENS cells were descendants of a common proliferating progenitor (Figure 6G).
evidence: Mathematical modeling comparing observed and simulated cell densities (Figure 6G).

claim: The observed homotypic and heterotypic clusters of EdU+ ENS cells were descendants of a common proliferating progenitor.
source: This analysis revealed that the actual densities of GFP+EdU+ and HuC/D+ EdU+ cells were significantly higher within the smaller radius circles (<60 µm from the cell of interest) in comparison to those expected by chance, suggesting that the observed homotypic (GFP+EdU+/GFP+EdU+) and heterotypic (GFP+EdU+/HuC/D+EdU+) clusters of EdU+ ENS cells were descendants of a common proliferating progenitor (Figure 6G).
evidence: Inferred from mathematical modeling showing non-random clustering of EdU+ cells (Figure 6G).

claim: The percentage of enteric neurons labelled by EdU (Cherry+HuC/D+EdU+) at t4 and t11 was higher relative to t0 in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) transgenics.
source: Consistent with our previous analysis (Figure 6E), the percentage of enteric neurons labelled by EdU (Cherry+HuC/D+EdU+) at t4 and t11 was higher relative to t0 (t0: 0.021 ± 0.15%; t4: 0.28 ± 1.2%, p=0.06; t11: 0.37 ± 0.95%, p=0.0014) (Figure 6H).
evidence: Quantification from EdU chase experiments in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish (Figure 6H).

claim: The percentage of EdU-labelled GFP- non-neuronal ENS cells (Cherry+GFP-HuC/D-EdU+) at t4 and t11 was higher relative to t0 in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) transgenics.
source: Interestingly, this increase was paralleled by an increased percentage of EdU-labelled GFP- non-neuronal ENS cells (Cherry+GFP-HuC/D-EdU+) at t4 and t11, relative to t0 (t0: 0.12 ± 0.5%; t4: 3.7 ± 12.5%, p=1.84×10−6; t11: 4.1 ± 15.5%, p=0.0024) (Figure 6I).
evidence: Quantification from EdU chase experiments in Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish (Figure 6I).

claim: Loss of Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expression in the daughters of proliferating EGCs is likely to reflect neurogenic commitment preceding overt neuronal differentiation.
source: Together these studies suggest that loss of Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expression in the daughters of proliferating EGCs is likely to reflect neurogenic commitment preceding overt neuronal differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cherry+GFP-HuC/D-EdU+ cells increase in parallel with Cherry+HuC/D+EdU+ cells (Figure 6H,I).

claim: Inhibition of Notch signalling promotes the proliferation and neurogenic differentiation of Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expressing RGCs in the telencephalon of zebrafish.
source: Inhibition of Notch signalling promotes the proliferation and neurogenic differentiation of Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expressing RGCs in the telencephalon of zebrafish (Alunni et al., 2013; Chapouton et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Alunni et al., 2013; Chapouton et al., 2010).

claim: LY treatment of Tg(her4.3:EGFP) zebrafish resulted in rapid loss of GFP signal from the gut.
source: As expected, LY treatment of Tg(her4.3:EGFP) zebrafish resulted in rapid loss of GFP signal from the gut (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from LY treatment experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Tg(her4.3:EGFP) is a bona fide target of canonical Notch signalling in the ENS.
source: Although this experiment confirmed that Tg(her4.3:EGFP) is a bona fide target of canonical Notch signalling in the ENS, it precluded the use of this transgene as a marker and lineage tracer of the EGC response to LY treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LY treatment caused loss of GFP signal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Notch inhibition in 3–4 month old Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish resulted in a dramatic increase in the percentage of non-neuronal ENS cells incorporating EdU (control: 0.0387 ± 0.21%; LY: 15.6 ± 17.0%, p=2.67×10−7).
source: As shown in Figure 7B, Notch inhibition in 3–4 month old Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish resulted in a dramatic increase in the percentage of non-neuronal ENS cells incorporating EdU (Cherry+HuC/D-EdU+) (control: 0.0387 ± 0.21%; LY: 15.6 ± 17.0%, p=2.67×10−7).
evidence: Quantification from LY treatment experiments (Figure 7B).

claim: A robust proliferative response of non-neuronal ENS cells was observed in 6 month old Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) animals following Notch inhibition (control: 0.832 ± 1.87%; LY: 6.95 ± 8.2%, p=1.98×10−5).
source: A robust proliferative response of non-neuronal ENS cells was also observed in 6 month old Tg(sox10:Cre;Cherry) animals (control: 0.832 ± 1.87%; LY: 6.95 ± 8.2%, p=1.98×10−5) (Figure 7D).
evidence: Quantification from LY treatment experiments (Figure 7D).

claim: LY treatment resulted in increased enteric neurogenesis in 3 month old animals (control: 0.0330 ± 0.18%; LY: 2.12 ± 7.8%, p=3.70×10−4).
source: Interestingly, LY treatment also resulted in increased enteric neurogenesis (Cherry+HuC/D+EdU+ cells) in both 3 month old (control: 0.0330 ± 0.18%; LY: 2.12 ± 7.8%, p=3.70×10−4) and 6 month old (control: 0.0652 ± 0.22%; LY: 1.56 ± 3.8%, 3.81 × 10−4) animals (Figure 7C,E).
evidence: Quantification from LY treatment experiments (Figure 7C).

claim: LY treatment resulted in increased enteric neurogenesis in 6 month old animals (control: 0.0652 ± 0.22%; LY: 1.56 ± 3.8%, p=3.81 × 10−4).
source: Interestingly, LY treatment also resulted in increased enteric neurogenesis (Cherry+HuC/D+EdU+ cells) in both 3 month old (control: 0.0330 ± 0.18%; LY: 2.12 ± 7.8%, p=3.70×10−4) and 6 month old (control: 0.0652 ± 0.22%; LY: 1.56 ± 3.8%, 3.81 × 10−4) animals (Figure 7C,E).
evidence: Quantification from LY treatment experiments (Figure 7E).

claim: Notch signalling regulates the dynamics of EGCs in the vertebrate gut throughout life.
source: Irrespective of the exact mechanisms, our experiments demonstrate that, similar to pallial RGCs (Alunni et al., 2013), Notch signalling regulates the dynamics of EGCs in the vertebrate gut throughout life.
evidence: Demonstrated by LY treatment experiments showing increased proliferation and neurogenesis in both 3-4 and 6-7 month old zebrafish (Figure 7B-E).

claim: In vertebrates, assembly of the ENS begins during embryogenesis with invasion of the foregut by a small founder population of neural crest (NC) cells.
source: In vertebrates, assembly of the ENS begins during embryogenesis with invasion of the foregut by a small founder population of neural crest (NC) cells that proliferate and colonise the entire GI tract, generating diverse types of enteric neurons and glial cells organised into networks of interconnected ganglia (Heanue and Pachnis, 2007).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Heanue and Pachnis, 2007).

claim: NC cells proliferate and colonise the entire GI tract, generating diverse types of enteric neurons and glial cells organised into networks of interconnected ganglia.
source: In vertebrates, assembly of the ENS begins during embryogenesis with invasion of the foregut by a small founder population of neural crest (NC) cells that proliferate and colonise the entire GI tract, generating diverse types of enteric neurons and glial cells organised into networks of interconnected ganglia (Heanue and Pachnis, 2007).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Heanue and Pachnis, 2007).

claim: The vast majority of enteric neurons in the mammalian ENS are born during embryogenesis and early postnatal stages and remain functionally integrated into the intestinal circuitry throughout life.
source: The predominant view holds that the vast majority of enteric neurons in the mammalian ENS are born during embryogenesis and early postnatal stages and remain functionally integrated into the intestinal circuitry throughout life (Bergner et al., 2014; Joseph et al., 2011; Laranjeira et al., 2011; Pham et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Bergner et al., 2014; Joseph et al., 2011; Laranjeira et al., 2011; Pham et al., 1991).

claim: Mammalian enteric glial cells (EGCs) are generally quiescent, with only a small fraction proliferating at any given time.
source: Likewise, enteric glial cells (EGCs) are generally quiescent, with only a small fraction proliferating at any given time (Joseph et al., 2011; Kabouridis et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Joseph et al., 2011; Kabouridis et al., 2015).

claim: Under experimental conditions such as chemical injury and bacterial infection, a small fraction of Sox10+ and Sox2+ EGCs can differentiate into neurons in mice.
source: Despite this static view of the ENS at homeostasis, lineage tracing experiments in mice have provided evidence that under experimental conditions, such as chemical injury of the ganglionic plexus and bacterial infection, a small fraction of Sox10+ and Sox2+ EGCs can differentiate into neurons (Belkind-Gerson et al., 2017; Belkind-Gerson et al., 2015; Laranjeira et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Belkind-Gerson et al., 2017; Belkind-Gerson et al., 2015; Laranjeira et al., 2011).

claim: A recent study argued that a population of Sox10-Nestin+ ENS cells undergo extensive proliferation and neuronal differentiation even under physiological conditions.
source: However, a recent study has argued that a population of Sox10-Nestin+ ENS cells undergo extensive proliferation and neuronal differentiation even under physiological conditions, replenishing enteric neurons continuously lost to apoptosis (Kulkarni et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Kulkarni et al., 2017).

claim: Fundamental tenets of the proposition that Sox10-Nestin+ ENS cells undergo extensive proliferation and neuronal differentiation under physiological conditions are not supported by available experimental evidence.
source: Although fundamental tenets of this proposition are not supported by available experimental evidence (Joseph et al., 2011; Laranjeira et al., 2011; White et al., 2018), it highlights critical but unresolved questions regarding the cellular and molecular mechanisms underpinning the maintenance and regenerative potential of the ENS in vertebrates.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Joseph et al., 2011; Laranjeira et al., 2011; White et al., 2018).

claim: Mammalian enteric glia are remarkably similar to protoplasmic astrocytes and express the intermediate filament GFAP.
source: Earlier histological studies demonstrated that mammalian enteric glia are remarkably similar to protoplasmic astrocytes and express the intermediate filament GFAP, a characteristic astrocytic marker (Jessen and Mirsky, 1980; Rühl, 2005).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Jessen and Mirsky, 1980; Rühl, 2005).

claim: Four morphological subtypes of mammalian enteric glia have been identified, which correlate with their position in the gut and relative to the ganglionic network.
source: Extending these early reports, we and others have identified four morphological subtypes of mammalian enteric glia, which correlate with their position in the gut and relative to the ganglionic network in the gut wall (Boesmans et al., 2015; Gulbransen and Sharkey, 2012; Hanani and Reichenbach, 1994).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Boesmans et al., 2015; Gulbransen and Sharkey, 2012; Hanani and Reichenbach, 1994).

claim: GFAP is normally detected in a subpopulation of mammalian EGCs in vivo.
source: In support of this idea, GFAP is dynamic and is normally detected in a subpopulation of mammalian EGCs in vivo (Boesmans et al., 2015) and expression of GFAP and S100b is enhanced in primary cultures of human enteric glia challenged with pro-inflammatory stimuli (Cirillo et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Boesmans et al., 2015; Cirillo et al., 2011).

claim: Expression of GFAP and S100b is enhanced in primary cultures of human enteric glia challenged with pro-inflammatory stimuli.
source: In support of this idea, GFAP is dynamic and is normally detected in a subpopulation of mammalian EGCs in vivo (Boesmans et al., 2015) and expression of GFAP and S100b is enhanced in primary cultures of human enteric glia challenged with pro-inflammatory stimuli (Cirillo et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Cirillo et al., 2011).

claim: The increased capacity for neural processing of the brain in higher vertebrates has been fuelled during evolution by the increased number, size and complexity of astrocytes.
source: A series of studies demonstrating that glial cells regulate synaptic activity of CNS neural circuits have led to the suggestion that the enhanced capacity for neural processing of the brain in higher vertebrates has been fuelled during evolution by the increased number, size and complexity of astrocytes (Han et al., 2013; Oberheim et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Han et al., 2013; Oberheim et al., 2006).

claim: The higher number of enteric glia in mammals, relative to teleosts, may reflect an increase in the functional complexity of intestinal neural circuits during vertebrate evolution.
source: Perhaps the higher number of enteric glia in mammals, relative to teleosts, may also reflect an increase in the functional complexity of intestinal neural circuits during vertebrate evolution and an enhanced scope of EGCs in the regulation of the complex gut tissue circuitry that maintains epithelial cell homeostasis, host defence and healthy microbiota (Grubišić and Gulbransen, 2017).
evidence: Speculative inference based on comparison to CNS astrocytes and cited literature (Grubišić and Gulbransen, 2017).

claim: Schwann cell precursors (SCPs) associated with growing nerves in mammalian embryos function as multipotent progenitors giving rise to diverse cell types.
source: For example, Schwann cell precursors (SCPs) associated with growing nerves in mammalian embryos, in addition to generating the Schwann cell lineage of adult animals, also function as multipotent progenitors giving rise to diverse cell types, including mesenchymal and neuroendocrine cells, parasympathetic neurons and melanocytes (Parfejevs et al., 2018; Petersen and Adameyko, 2017).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Parfejevs et al., 2018; Petersen and Adameyko, 2017).

claim: ENS progenitors already expressing molecular markers attributed to EGCs are capable of generating enteric neurons and mature enteric glia.
source: Echoing the developmental potential of SCPs, ENS progenitors already expressing molecular markers attributed to EGCs are also capable of generating enteric neurons and mature enteric glia (Cooper et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 2017; Lasrado et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Cooper et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 2017; Lasrado et al., 2017).

claim: NCSC properties can be acquired by peripheral glia cell lineages from adult animals, including Schwann cells, glia of the carotid body and EGCs.
source: In addition to these studies, a growing body of evidence indicates that NCSC properties can be acquired by peripheral glia cell lineages from adult animals, including Schwann cells, glia of the carotid body and EGCs (Jessen et al., 2015; Pardal et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Jessen et al., 2015; Pardal et al., 2007).

claim: Reprogramming of differentiated glial cells into a NCSC-state is generally induced by injury, infection or other types of stress.
source: However, it is generally thought that the reprogramming of differentiated glial cells into a NCSC-state is induced by injury, infection or other types of stress, including tissue dissociation and culture.
evidence: General knowledge from the field.

claim: The neurogenic potential of mammalian enteric glia disclosed under conditions of injury and stress reflects an earlier evolutionary state of anamniote vertebrates.
source: By providing evidence that zebrafish EGCs, in addition to their bona fide role as glial cells, also serve as constitutive ENS progenitors in vivo, our studies argue that the neurogenic potential of mammalian enteric glia disclosed under conditions of injury and stress, reflects an earlier evolutionary state of anamniote vertebrates, in which the same cell type exhibited properties of neural progenitors and mature glia.
evidence: Inferred from the findings of this study showing constitutive neurogenesis by zebrafish EGCs.

claim: Peripheral glia lineages in lower vertebrates represent NCSCs that retain their developmental options but adjust to the cellular environment by acquiring additional specialised functions.
source: Although it is currently unclear whether neurogenic potential is a unique property of teleost EGCs, we speculate that peripheral glia lineages in lower vertebrates represent NCSCs that retain their developmental options but adjust to the cellular environment they reside in by acquiring additional specialised functions that contribute to local tissue function and homeostasis.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Zebrafish EGCs show remarkable and unexpected parallels to RGCs, NSCs that are distributed widely in teleost brain.
source: By subsuming features of both neural progenitors and glial cells, zebrafish EGCs show remarkable and unexpected parallels to RGCs, NSCs that are distributed widely in teleost brain, reflecting its pronounced neurogenic and regenerative potential (Alunni and Bally-Cuif, 2016; Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015), and take on functions normally attributed to astrocytes (Lyons and Talbot, 2015).
evidence: Comparison to RGCs based on findings of this study and cited literature (Alunni and Bally-Cuif, 2016; Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015; Lyons and Talbot, 2015).

claim: RGCs are NSCs that are distributed widely in teleost brain, reflecting its pronounced neurogenic and regenerative potential.
source: By subsuming features of both neural progenitors and glial cells, zebrafish EGCs show remarkable and unexpected parallels to RGCs, NSCs that are distributed widely in teleost brain, reflecting its pronounced neurogenic and regenerative potential (Alunni and Bally-Cuif, 2016; Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015), and take on functions normally attributed to astrocytes (Lyons and Talbot, 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Alunni and Bally-Cuif, 2016; Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015).

claim: RGCs take on functions normally attributed to astrocytes.
source: By subsuming features of both neural progenitors and glial cells, zebrafish EGCs show remarkable and unexpected parallels to RGCs, NSCs that are distributed widely in teleost brain, reflecting its pronounced neurogenic and regenerative potential (Alunni and Bally-Cuif, 2016; Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015), and take on functions normally attributed to astrocytes (Lyons and Talbot, 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Lyons and Talbot, 2015).

claim: The majority of EGCs remain quiescent at steady state (qEGCs).
source: Thus, similar to RGCs, the majority of EGCs remain quiescent at steady state (qEGCs), but in response to as yet unknown signals, a proportion of them enters the cell cycle giving rise to active EGCs (aEGCs).
evidence: Proposed model based on findings showing ~10% of EGCs are proliferative (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: In response to as yet unknown signals, a proportion of qEGCs enters the cell cycle giving rise to active EGCs (aEGCs).
source: Thus, similar to RGCs, the majority of EGCs remain quiescent at steady state (qEGCs), but in response to as yet unknown signals, a proportion of them enters the cell cycle giving rise to active EGCs (aEGCs).
evidence: Proposed model based on findings showing proliferative EGCs (Figure 6).

claim: Extinction of Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expression is associated with irreversible commitment of aEGCs to enteric neural progenitors (eNPs).
source: Extinction of Tg(her4.3:EGFP) expression is associated with irreversible commitment of aEGCs to enteric neural progenitors (eNPs), which eventually differentiate to mature enteric neurons capable of integration into functional intestinal neural circuits.
evidence: Proposed model based on findings showing loss of GFP preceding neuronal differentiation (Figure 6C).

claim: The transient population of eNPs correspond to the HuC/D-GFP- cells identified in the ENS of Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish.
source: We suggest that this transient population of eNPs correspond to the HuC/D-GFP- cells identified in the ENS of Tg(her4.3:EGFP;sox10:Cre;Cherry) zebrafish (Figure 3B).
evidence: Proposed interpretation of the Cherry+HuC/D-GFP- cell population (Figure 3B).

claim: Notch signalling has been implicated in the development of the mammalian ENS by inhibiting the intrinsic neurogenic programme of ENS progenitors.
source: Notch signalling has also been implicated in the development of the mammalian ENS by inhibiting the intrinsic neurogenic programme of ENS progenitors (Okamura and Saga, 2008).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Okamura and Saga, 2008).

claim: The Notch activity reporter Tg(her4.3:EGFP) is activated in ENS progenitors shortly after they invade the gut and initiate neurogenic differentiation.
source: Our demonstration that the Notch activity reporter Tg(her4.3:EGFP) is activated in ENS progenitors shortly after they invade the gut and initiate neurogenic differentiation suggests a similar role of Notch signalling in the development of the zebrafish ENS, namely attenuation of the strong neurogenic bias of early ENS progenitors acquired as they enter the foregut and induce strong neurogenic transcription factors, such as Phox2B and Ascl1 (Charrier and Pilon, 2017).
evidence: Inferred from findings showing EGFP expression appearing at 60-62 hpf in post-migratory cells (Figure 5) and cited literature (Charrier and Pilon, 2017).
